query: Consider the following context: Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. In that context, which method can be used for overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, and why?

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: Early studies (2014) on eutectic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) demonstrated that a refined lamellar microstructure can yield simultaneous high strength and ductility. Subsequently (2018), inverted microstructures in refractory HEAs achieved further improvements by embedding coherent precipitates in a ductile matrix, raising both yield strength and fracture strain. Later work (2021) probed superplastic-like deformation in HEA nanowires, confirming that extended malleability and high flow stress can both be accessed by careful control of defect processes and phases. Most recently (2023), multiple coherent precipitation structures were tailored via stepwise thermo-mechanical processing, pushing strength-ductility combinations to new levels. Across these efforts, microstructure engineering – especially controlling phase and precipitate length scales – has repeatedly emerged as a key strategy for surpassing the usual trade-off between strength and ductility. Nevertheless, identifying the optimal pathways among a wide range of processing conditions remains challenging, because so many factors (e.g., processing temperatures, strain rates, annealing profiles) influence mechanical responses.
decision.unsolved: While hierarchical microstructures show promise, the field lacks efficient, systematic strategies for identifying the optimal thermo-mechanical parameters that balance strength and ductility in metal-based materials. Manually exploring vast process-structure-property relationships is laborious, and the best synergy often remains elusive without comprehensive, data-driven guidance.
decision.lever: Use a multi-parameter machine-learning framework to rapidly predict and optimize thermo-mechanical processing paths that maximize strength-ductility synergy, by correlating microstructural features (e.g., grain size, secondary phase distributions) with mechanical outcomes.
decision.why: This approach follows from the demonstrated importance of microstructural engineering in previous studies yet addresses the current challenge of exploring extensive parameter spaces. A targeted ML model can leverage existing data to pinpoint promising process windows for further experimental validation, accelerating the discovery of routes that overcome the strength-ductility trade-off.
